strengths: The paper offers a clean, unifying perspective: it frames inference-time control of diffusion models as classical (local + global) search and proves a genuine (if modest) theoretical unification — that training-free guidance with recurrence converges, in the continuous limit, to annealed Langevin MCMC (Proposition 1, with a reasonably careful derivation in Appendix C). This gives a principled account of why recurrence mitigates OOD/adversarial samples and connects previously disconnected lines of work (guidance, compositional generation, MCMC).

Breadth of evaluation is a clear strength: maze planning (including a new harder PointMaze Ultra variant), D4RL offline RL, CompBench text-to-image, and ImageNet conditional generation, with task-appropriate verifiers (world-model style verifier, pretrained Q-function, oracle VQA/detector verifiers, classifiers).

The compute-efficiency analysis is more systematic than much prior work: BFS-Resampling/BFS-Pruning and DFS are compared against Best-of-N on compute-matched curves, and the difficulty-adaptive compute allocation of DFS (Fig. 4c) is an interesting and useful property.

Practical touches are thoughtful: the double-verifier scheme to mitigate verifier hacking/adversarial examples, the observation about terminal-SNR issues when backtracking to t=T, and decoupling the transition kernel from the search strategy so both stochastic and deterministic samplers can be used.
Algorithms and pseudo-code (Algs. 1-4) plus hyperparameter tables make the methods largely reproducible.
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to closest prior work. BFS-resampling/pruning over particles is essentially particle filtering / Feynman-Kac steering / SMC ([62], [84], [99]) and the tree-search framing overlaps heavily with Ma et al. [48] and restart sampling [91]. The paper argues qualitatively that prior methods are 'instances' of the framework, but never runs a direct head-to-head empirical comparison against [48] or [62] on any shared benchmark — a significant gap given these are the main baselines the paper positions itself against.

The headline theoretical result (Prop. 1) is a fairly expected equivalence between recurrent denoise-then-renoise steps and Langevin dynamics, and much of the practical local search inherits its design space wholesale from TFG [94]; the marginal technical contribution over these components is thin.

Offline RL results do not support a superiority claim: the average (86.1) is slightly below QGPO (86.6), and Medium-Replay Walker2d (79.3 ± 9.7) is notably worse than D-QL (94.3) with very high variance. The method is 'competitive', not better; moreover, only Best-of-N with tiny particle counts (2-4) is used in RL, so the paper's main global-search machinery is untested in that domain.

ImageNet evaluation is weak: only two class labels (222, 444) with 256 samples per label — FID estimates at that sample size are unreliable, and FID values of 127-188 are far from typical operating points for conditional ImageNet generation, making it hard to assess practical value.

Local search requires a differentiable verifier, which excludes many of the most practically interesting verifiers (the text-to-image experiments are global-search-only for exactly this reason); the interplay or combined benefit of local and global search is only partially demonstrated, and no ablation isolates their individual contributions on the harder tasks.

Hyperparameter sensitivity is acknowledged but not resolved: extensive per-task grid searches over temperatures, thresholds, schedules, step sizes (Tables 3, App. E) undercut the 'training-free, plug-and-play' selling point, and no sensitivity analysis or automatic tuning is provided.

Several claims are stronger than the evidence: 'consistently surpass baselines in terms of compute efficiency' is shown only against Best-of-N (itself the weakest baseline), not against stronger verifier-guided or SMC-style methods; presentation also has multiple typos and grammatical issues (e.g., 'a instance', 'There zero-order search', 'procal', 'tha maze') that suggest insufficient polish.

Scalability of the search itself is not examined at modern scales: experiments use small models (SSD-1B, 256px DDPM, 16-100 step samplers) and modest particle counts, leaving open whether tree search remains compute-competitive for large text-to-image models where NFEs are far more expensive.

strengths: The paper offers a clean conceptual framing of inference-time search in diffusion models, decomposing methods into local search (gradient/Langevin-based) and global search (BFS/DFS over the denoising tree), which is intuitive and helps organize a rapidly growing literature.

Proposition 1, showing that training-free guidance with recurrence is an instance of annealed Langevin MCMC in the continuous limit, is a useful unifying observation that provides practical insight (e.g., reusing the TFG hyperparameter design space) and explains why naive gradient ascent produces OOD samples (Sec. C.4).

The evaluation spans multiple domains (maze planning, offline RL on D4RL, text-to-image on CompBench, ImageNet conditional generation), and the paper is generally well written with clear algorithmic descriptions and pseudo-code in the appendix.

The BFS-Pruning/Resampling and DFS variants are sensible compute-allocation strategies, and the demonstration that DFS adaptively allocates compute based on prompt difficulty (Fig. 4c) is a nice empirical observation.
The proposed offline RL approach is training-free, which is a practical advantage over QGPO/Diffusion-QL style methods that require training noise-dependent energy functions.
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to prior work. The core building blocks are largely known: BFS-style particle resampling/pruning over diffusion denoising is essentially SMC/Feynman-Kac steering [62, 84, 99] and closely related to Ma et al. [48]; the local search component is training-free guidance with recurrence [94, 95]. The main novelty is the framing/unification and Proposition 1, whose proof (Sec. C.3.1) is a straightforward continuous-limit argument rather than a deep theoretical result.

Missing direct empirical comparison to the closest prior work. Despite framing Ma et al. [48] as the main related method, the experiments do not include a head-to-head comparison with their inference-time search algorithms under matched compute, which is essential to substantiate the claim that gradient-based local search is 'crucial' and more efficient. Similarly, no comparison with SMC-based steering methods [62].

The offline RL results do not actually surpass the strongest baselines: the average score (86.1) is below QGPO (86.6) and D-QL (86.3), and per-task results are mostly within noise. The claim of 'competitive performance' is defensible, but the framing overstates the contribution; the advantage is essentially 'training-free at similar performance.'

The ImageNet conditional generation experiments are small-scale: only two class labels (222 and 444) with 256 samples each, and FID computed against class-specific ImageNet subsets. Conclusions about BFS efficiency from such a narrow, high-variance setting are weakly supported; a broader label set or standard benchmark protocol is needed.

The double-verifier mechanism (Sec. 5.3.2) is introduced in an ad hoc manner, inspired by double Q-learning, with no analysis of when or why it mitigates verifier hacking, and it is only evaluated in the Best-of-N setting of Table 2.

Hyperparameter sensitivity is significant and acknowledged only in limitations: grid searches over guidance strengths, temperatures, thresholds, evaluation steps, and backtracking depths are performed per task/dataset (Tables 3, Sec. D.1-D.2, E.1-E.3). This weakens the 'practical and principled foundation' claim and raises fairness concerns versus baselines with fixed settings; the paper itself notes more tuning is needed than training-based methods.

Several key claims rely on qualitative or lightly-supported evidence: e.g., efficiency gains over Best-of-N are shown via plots (Figs. 3-5) without consistent quantitative tables, error bars, or matched-NREs reporting, making it difficult to assess the magnitude and significance of the efficiency improvements.

The DFS threshold schedule delta_t and its interaction with verifier calibration is under-analyzed; DFS behavior (backtracking frequency, performance) likely depends strongly on verifier score distributions at intermediate noise levels, and the paper offers no analysis of this calibration issue, which is central to the method's practicality.

strengths: The paper presents a clean and well-motivated unification of inference-time search for diffusion models, organizing prior gradient-based guidance and particle/tree-based methods as instances of local search (Langevin MCMC) and global search (BFS/DFS) over the denoising chain. Proposition 1, showing that training-free guidance with recurrence is equivalent to Langevin MCMC on an annealed sequence of distributions in the continuous limit, is a genuine and useful theoretical contribution that explains why recurrence mitigates OOD/adversarial samples (via the KL decomposition in Appendix C.4).

Evaluation breadth is a major strength: the framework is instantiated across three distinct domains (long-horizon maze planning with a physics-grounded verifier, offline RL on D4RL locomotion with a Q-function verifier, and text-to-image/conditional ImageNet generation), demonstrating generality of the search abstraction that decouples the transition kernel from the search strategy.

The compute-efficiency analyses are convincing and go beyond simple performance tables: BFS-Resampling/BFS-Pruning and DFS consistently outperform Best-of-N at matched compute (Figs. 3e-f, 4, 5), and the demonstration that DFS adaptively allocates compute by prompt difficulty without prior knowledge (Fig. 4c) is an interesting and practically relevant finding.

Practical touches add credibility: the double-verifier scheme to mitigate verifier hacking is a nice, well-motivated idea (Table 2), the observation about nonzero terminal SNR causing cumulative errors upon full backtracking is a useful engineering insight, and the appendices provide detailed algorithms, hyperparameters, and seed-separated hyperparameter search/evaluation for D4RL.
The paper is clearly written, well-structured, and positions itself honestly relative to closest concurrent work (Ma et al. [48], FK steering [62]), explaining what the new framework adds.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: the individual algorithmic components are largely existing—local search is essentially training-free guidance with recurrence ([94, 95]), and global search via particle resampling/pruning closely resembles Sequential Monte Carlo / Feynman-Kac steering [62] and the particle-based methods of Ma et al. [48]. The main contribution is the unification and the Langevin interpretation rather than fundamentally new machinery, which limits the conceptual advance over prior art.

There is no head-to-head empirical comparison against the closest prior inference-time scaling methods (Ma et al. [48] or FK steering [62]), despite the paper claiming superior compute efficiency. Comparisons are primarily against naive Best-of-N, which weakens the central claim that the proposed framework is more efficient than existing search-based approaches.

The offline RL results are competitive rather than superior: the average score (86.1) is slightly below QGPO (86.6), Medium-Replay Walker2d (79.3) lags D-QL (94.3) substantially, and baseline numbers are taken directly from [44] rather than re-run under controlled conditions.

The ImageNet conditional generation evaluation is narrow: only two class labels (222 and 444) with 256 samples per label, and FID computed against only those classes. This is a very limited basis for claims about conditional generation scaling, and raises concerns about selection of favorable settings.

The method requires substantial per-task hyperparameter tuning (grid searches over temperature, thresholds, backtracking depth, evaluation schedules, per-task verifier designs), which the authors acknowledge in the limitations; this reduces practicality and makes the 'training-free' advantage relative to methods like QGPO less decisive.

Some claims are stated more strongly than the evidence supports, e.g., 'we are the first to propose this theoretical unification' rests on a continuous-limit argument whose assumptions (T → ∞, specific sampler forms) may not hold for the few-step samplers actually used in experiments; also the project page link in the abstract appears broken, affecting reproducibility claims.

The theoretical results are qualitative connections without quantitative guarantees (no analysis of compute-performance tradeoffs, convergence under the practical discretization, or when global search provably helps), and the BFS resampling formula lacks any theoretical justification for why proportional-to-score allocation is appropriate.

strengths: Comprehensive unification: the paper provides a clean design space (tempering, scoring, resampling) that recovers prior particle/tree-based methods (SVDD, DAS, FK-steering, TreeG) as special cases of a BFS framework, and systematically ablates design choices with meaningful gains on both SD v1.5 and SDXL.

The theoretical contribution connecting training-free guidance with recurrence to annealed Langevin MCMC (Prop. 1, Theorem 1) is a genuinely useful unification that explains why recurrence mitigates OOD/reward-hacking artifacts, and is supported by a detailed derivation and convergence analysis.

Breadth and quality of evaluation is a major strength: text-to-image (ImageReward, CompBench), long-horizon maze planning, D4RL offline RL, and ImageNet conditional generation, with Pareto-curve style compute-normalized comparisons and appropriate baselines including TFG and DAS given generous compute allowances.
The adaptive DFS with verifier-threshold backtracking is a practical contribution: it dynamically allocates compute by instance difficulty and is shown to outperform BFS and BoN at reduced cost.

Additional valuable results beyond the main claims, including expert iteration/policy distillation beating DPPO with a simple offline procedure, and a double-verifier strategy that empirically reduces reward hacking with better FID/accuracy/MSP trade-offs.
Extensive appendices with full pseudocode, hyperparameter tables, and experiment details support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: the BFS framework largely packages existing SMC/particle methods, and key improvements (SSP resampling from Gerber et al., tempering from DAS, max scoring from FK-steering) are borrowed or recombined. The DFS is a fairly straightforward threshold-based backtracking heuristic, and local search closely follows Du et al. (2023)'s annealed Langevin composition.

The theoretical results rest on restrictive assumptions (bounded support, strong log-concavity, smoothness) that plainly do not hold for realistic diffusion models and verifiers, so the 'rigorous convergence bound' has limited practical force; claims of 'asymptotically exact sampling' should be softened.

The claim of being 'first to jointly scale local and global search' is overstated given Ma et al. (2025) explored a combination of local zero-order search and global path search; the concurrent-work discussion mitigates but does not fully resolve this.

Potential circularity in evaluation: ImageReward is used both as the search verifier and as the implicit success metric for SD v1.5/SDXL experiments, which inflates gains and does not demonstrate improvement in actual generation quality; no human evaluation or independent image metric is reported for the main text-to-image results.
The double-verifier ImageNet study is small-scale (FID on only 256 samples, which is statistically unreliable) and is the only evidence for a component given significant space in the main text.

D4RL results are comparable rather than superior (average 86.1 vs. 86.6 QGPO and 86.3 D-QL), and the best-of-N with only 2-4 particles makes the offline RL gains modest; Walker2d Medium-Replay variance is very high (±9.7).

The local search experiments depend on extensive hyperparameter searches (ρ̄, μ̄ magnitudes and step sizes), and the paper acknowledges inference scaling 'still requires additional hyperparameters' without a robustness analysis of sensitivity.

strengths: The paper provides a useful unification: showing that prior particle/tree-based inference-scaling methods (SVDD, DAS, FK-steering, TreeG) are special cases of a single BFS design space (tempering, scoring, resampling) is a genuine contribution to understanding the literature, and the resulting improved BFS configuration is supported by clean ablations (Table 1) and cross-model comparisons (Table 2).

The adaptive DFS algorithm with verifier-threshold-driven backtracking is a simple but interesting idea, and the experiments demonstrating automatic compute allocation by prompt difficulty (Fig. 3 right) are compelling and relevant to the broader test-time-compute conversation.

The theoretical observation that training-free guidance with recurrence is equivalent to annealed Langevin MCMC in the continuous-time limit (Prop. 1, Thm. 1) is a nice conceptual link that explains empirically observed OOD/reward-hacking phenomena.

Evaluation spans multiple domains (text-to-image, maze planning, offline RL, conditional ImageNet generation), baselines are mostly recent and fairly tuned (e.g., baselines given up to 2x compute in the RL setting), and the double-verifier experiment on reward hacking addresses a practically important failure mode.
The appendices are unusually thorough, with full pseudocode, derivations, and hyperparameter tables that support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty at the component level: the 'improved BFS' is largely a recombination of known ingredients (SSP resampling from Gerber et al., tempering from DAS, max scoring from FK-steering), and the 'new' local search is essentially TFG with recurrence already described in Ye et al. (2024). The contribution rests heavily on the framing/unification rather than a fundamentally new technique.

The theory is weak in practice: Theorem 1 assumes bounded support, strong log-concavity, and smoothness of q~t — assumptions that plainly fail for the multimodal, complex distributions the paper targets (the same distributions the authors cite as motivation). The bound therefore offers little practical guarantee, and the paper's claim of a 'rigorous convergence bound' overstates its applicability.

Some evaluation is thin or potentially misleading: FID computed on only 256 samples (Table 5) is statistically unreliable; several results use only 4 seeds; Table 3 uses a generous 'within 5% of maximum' presentation although the average (86.1) does not clearly beat training-based baselines (QGPO 86.6, D-QL 86.3); and the double-verifier idea is validated on only a single task.

Key methods introduce new hyperparameters (DFS thresholds δt, backtracking depth, tempering γ) whose sensitivity is only partially studied; the limitation section admits this but offers no mitigation beyond deferring to future 'evolutionary search' heuristics.

The reward-hacking mitigation is heuristic: the double-verifier strategy is borrowed loosely from double-Q learning without theoretical justification, and it is unclear why two independently trained classifiers would not be adversarially exploitable jointly.

Presentation issues undercut polish: typos ('Parero', 'successfual', 'inheritability biased'), a broken project-page link in the abstract, duplicate/ambiguous citations (Singhal et al. 2025a vs 2025b are the same work), and the abbreviation 'TTS' (test-time search) colliding with standard usage.

The core empirical gains, while consistent, are modest in several settings (e.g., Table 2 improvements over DAS are within roughly one standard error), which weakens the claim of establishing 'a new Pareto frontier.'

strengths: Comprehensive and unified framework: the paper cleanly maps particle-based SMC methods (SVDD, DAS, FK-steering, TreeG) into a single BFS design space (tempering, scoring, resampling), which both clarifies prior work and enables a genuinely improved configuration (Increase, Max, SSP) that consistently outperforms prior methods across two models (SD v1.5, SDXL) and compute budgets (Tables 1-2).

Meaningful theoretical contribution: Proposition 1 and Theorem 1 unify recurrent training-free guidance with annealed Langevin MCMC in the continuous-time limit, providing the first rigorous explanation of why recurrence mitigates OOD/adversarial samples in gradient guidance (App. C), and connecting two previously disjoint lines of work.

The adaptive DFS with verifier-driven backtracking is a novel and practically valuable mechanism: it allocates compute by instance difficulty without prior knowledge (Fig. 3), and shows up to 2x compute savings over BFS/BoN, addressing a real weakness of fixed-schedule particle methods.

Breadth of evaluation across challenging domains: text-to-image (CompBench with a VLM verifier), long-horizon PointMaze planning, offline RL on D4RL locomotion with strong baselines (IQL, D-QL, QGPO, Diffuser, TFG, DAS), and ImageNet conditional generation with FID/accuracy/MSP.

Several genuinely interesting secondary contributions: the double-verifier strategy to mitigate reward hacking (Table 5 shows simultaneous gains in FID, accuracy, and MSP), and the expert-iteration/policy-distillation result (Table 4) outperforming DPPO with a simple offline finetuning, which is of independent interest.

Good experimental hygiene: fair compute accounting in NFEs, ablations that vary one design choice at a time, hyperparameter search on separate seeds/datasets from evaluation, and honest reporting of search-set vs. eval-set performance (Table 9).
weaknesses: The improved BFS is largely a recombination of components already present in prior work (Increase tempering from DAS, Max scoring from FK-steering, SSP resampling from Kim et al.), so the headline empirical gains in Table 2 are incremental (e.g., 1.087 vs. 1.052 for DAS at N=8). The novelty rests more on the unification and the DFS/joint-scaling pieces than on the BFS design itself.

The convergence analysis (Theorem 1) assumes strong log-concavity, L-log-smoothness, and bounded support, conditions clearly violated by realistic multimodal diffusion targets; the authors themselves note ULA only converges to the 'concave vicinity' in multimodal cases. The theory is elegant but of limited direct relevance to the practical settings evaluated.

Offline RL results are competitive but not clearly superior: the TTS average (86.1) is slightly below D-QL (86.3) and QGPO (86.6), with high variance on some tasks (Walker2d Medium-Replay: 79.3 ± 9.7). Claims of matching training-based methods are fair but should be stated more cautiously, and the method relies on access to a separately trained Q-function.

Potential verifier-evaluation circularity: in the SD v1.5/SDXL experiments, ImageReward is used both as the search verifier and effectively the reported metric; the CompBench DFS results report 'Score' curves rather than human evaluation or an independent metric, so reward over-optimization cannot be ruled out in the image experiments (partially addressed only in Sec. 5.4).
FID computed on only 256 samples (Table 5) is statistically unreliable; conclusions about the double-verifier would be more convincing with larger sample sizes and confidence intervals.

The framework introduces many hyperparameters (tempering, thresholds δt, backtracking depth ΔT, guidance strengths ρ̄/μ̄, schedules); while ablations help, sensitivity analysis across domains is incomplete, and the limitations section acknowledges this only briefly.

The 'first to jointly scale local and global search' claim needs softening: concurrent works discussed in App. B.1 (e.g., ABCD, Ma et al. 2025 combining zero-order local and global path search) overlap substantially, and the paper's differentiation from them is mostly about principled framing and efficiency rather than a fundamentally new capability.
